exercises.english: She has had a fever since yesterday and keeps coughing – conclude that she is ill.
exercises.german: Sie muss krank sein.
exercises.why: Müssen in the epistemic use draws the conclusion that the symptoms indicate.

exercises.english: The street outside is completely wet, although the window is open – conclude that it rained.
exercises.german: Es hat geregnet.
exercises.why: Here the deduction needs no modal at all: a present perfect states what must have happened.

exercises.english: All three lights are on and nobody answers the phone – conclude that they are still at the office.
exercises.german: Sie müssen noch im Büro sein.
exercises.why: The plural subject confirms that the deduction is about all of them together.

exercises.english: He has eaten nothing since breakfast and keeps looking at the clock – conclude that he is hungry.
exercises.german: Er muss Hunger haben.
exercises.why: A deduction with a non-verbal conclusion, which is the standard müssen pattern.

exercises.english: Her face is pale and she has been in bed all afternoon – conclude that she is not feeling well.
exercises.german: Sie muss sich nicht wohlfühlen.
exercises.why: A deduction with a separable verb stays in the infinitive at the end of the clause.

exercises.english: Nobody has answered the bell for five minutes – conclude that the flat is empty.
exercises.german: Die Wohnung muss leer sein.
exercises.why: Müssen plus an adjective in the predicate states the inferred conclusion.

exercises.english: The file is nowhere in the folder, but she used it this morning – conclude that she deleted it.
exercises.german: Sie muss die Datei gelöscht haben.
exercises.why: The perfect infinitive locates the deduction in the past without changing the present modal.

exercises.english: The printer is switched on and the queue has not moved – conclude that the paper is jammed.
exercises.german: Es muss ein Papierstau sein.
exercises.why: Müssen with a nominal conclusion works as readily as one with an adjective.

exercises.english: His colleagues are still at their desks although the meeting started ten minutes ago – conclude that he is being waited for.
exercises.german: Man muss auf ihn warten.
exercises.why: With the impersonal man, the deduction no longer needs a subject in the nominative.

exercises.english: He has been calling the number for an hour without an answer – conclude that the number is wrong.
exercises.german: Die Nummer muss falsch sein.
exercises.why: The conclusion comes first in subject position, the evidence in a preceding prepositional phrase.

exercises.english: The official statement promises an answer this week – report it as given.
exercises.german: Laut der Pressemitteilung soll in dieser Woche eine Antwort kommen.
exercises.why: Sollen after laut attributes the conclusion to a written source.

exercises.english: The rumour says the department will close – report the rumour without committing to it.
exercises.german: Es heißt, die Abteilung werde geschlossen.
exercises.why: Hier a paraphrase frame carries the reported claim, keeping the speaker neutral.

exercises.english: The examiner is said to have marked the scripts already – state it as reported.
exercises.german: Der Prüfer soll die Klausuren schon korrigiert haben.
exercises.why: Reported deduction with sollen in the perfect and the participle placed at the end.

exercises.english: According to the technician, the fault must be in the cable – give the reported version.
exercises.german: Laut dem Techniker müsste der Fehler im Kabel liegen.
exercises.why: Konjunktiv II müsste plus laut marks the conclusion as somebody else's and fallible.

exercises.english: The absence list is signed by three people – conclude that they have not returned yet.
exercises.german: Die drei müssen noch auf dem Weg sein.
exercises.why: A numeral subject with müssen gives a deduction about their current state.

exercises.english: The manuscript is full of empty phrases – conclude that the author took no time for it.
exercises.german: Der Autor muss sich keine Zeit genommen haben.
exercises.why: The deduction carries a perfect infinitive with a verb taking a separable zu-infinitive.

exercises.english: Nothing was stolen but the safe is open – conclude that someone knew the code.
exercises.german: Jemand muss den Code gekannt haben.
exercises.why: Müssen here concludes that a hidden premise was met, a typical inference from lack of damage.

exercises.english: The date on the letter is from June – conclude that the notice is out of date.
exercises.german: Die Mitteilung muss veraltet sein.
exercises.why: Müssen with a temporal piece of evidence supports a state that still holds.

exercises.english: The train stopped for ten minutes in the middle of nowhere – conclude that there was a problem on the line.
exercises.german: Es muss auf der Strecke ein Problem gegeben haben.
exercises.why: The conclusion is a whole subordinate-style clause with a perfect infinitive and zu.

exercises.english: The sign says the museum is closed today, and there is no queue – conclude that nothing is open.
exercises.german: Es dürfte heute nichts geöffnet haben.
exercises.why: Dürfte plus perfect gives a probability estimate, the softest form of müssen.

exercises.english: Give your personal estimate that the train will arrive late again.
exercises.german: Meiner Meinung nach kommt der Zug wieder zu spät.
exercises.why: Meiner Meinung nach introduces a subjective assessment before the statement itself.

exercises.english: Say with certainty that the person at the door is a colleague.
exercises.german: Da ist sicher ein Kollege.
exercises.why: The emphatic sicher raises the certainty of an otherwise unqualified statement.

exercises.english: State your conclusion that she has not noticed anything, using a deduction modal and the perfect.
exercises.german: Sie muss nichts bemerkt haben.
exercises.why: Müssen in the epistemic use plus a perfect infinitive carries the deduction about a completed action.

exercises.english: Say that you assume the reason for the delay is technical.
exercises.german: Meiner Einschätzung nach ist der Grund für die Verspätung technisch bedingt.
exercises.why: Meiner Einschätzung nach introduces an inference in the main clause before the conclusion itself.

exercises.english: Express the possibility that the package went to the wrong address.
exercises.german: Das Paket könnte falsch adressiert worden sein.
exercises.why: Könnte plus perfect reports a possibility about the address without committing to a cause.

exercises.english: State as your own conclusion that they lost the key somewhere.
exercises.german: Sie haben den Schlüssel irgendwo verloren.
exercises.why: With an unmotivated present perfect, the present form itself expresses the deduction.

exercises.english: State your supposition that the hotel is fully booked.
exercises.german: Das Hotel ist vermutlich ausgebucht.
exercises.why: Vermutlich marks the speaker's estimate and needs no modal verb at all.

exercises.english: Express the possibility that the two lines are not connected.
exercises.german: Die beiden Linien könnten nicht verbunden sein.
exercises.why: Können combined with nicht covers a possibility the speaker doubts.

exercises.english: Say that you do not rule out the idea that the data were changed.
exercises.german: Man kann nicht ausschließen, dass die Daten geändert wurden.
exercises.why: The idiom man kann nicht ausschließen, dass introduces a possibility the speaker leaves open.

exercises.english: Give your personal opinion that the deadline is far too tight.
exercises.german: Die Frist ist meines Erachtens viel zu knapp.
exercises.why: Meines Erachtens is a formal way of marking a personal judgement.

exercises.english: Say, hedging your conclusion, that the date is probably correct after all.
exercises.german: Das Datum müsste doch stimmen.
exercises.why: Müsste presents the date as very probably correct, and doch adds the corrective stress.

exercises.english: State that you have the impression that nobody noticed.
exercises.german: Ich habe den Eindruck, dass es niemand bemerkt hat.
exercises.why: Ich habe den Eindruck, dass presents a conjecture as an impression, not as a fact.

exercises.english: Say that the file must have been corrupted, adding a hedge of your own.
exercises.german: Die Datei muss wohl beschädigt sein.
exercises.why: Wohl inside the clause softens an otherwise firm deduction.

exercises.english: Say that the meeting point could not have been the printed one.
exercises.german: Der Treffpunkt kann nicht der gedruckte gewesen sein.
exercises.why: Kann nicht rejects the alternative without naming a subject of ability.

exercises.english: Say that someone must have forgotten the extension cord.
exercises.german: Jemand muss das Verlängerungskabel vergessen haben.
exercises.why: A quantified subject plus müssen and perfect infinitive covers an unspecified person.

exercises.english: Give your opinion that the problem lies in the documentation.
exercises.german: Meiner Ansicht nach liegt das Problem in der Dokumentation.
exercises.why: Meiner Ansicht nach marks the following clause as the speaker's judgement.

exercises.english: State that the results could well arrive before Monday.
exercises.german: Die Ergebnisse könnten gut vor Montag kommen.
exercises.why: Gut as a focusing adverb raises the probability that könnte leaves open.

exercises.english: Say that you assume the majority has not noticed the change.
exercises.german: Die Mehrheit hat vermutlich die Änderung nicht bemerkt.
exercises.why: A negated clause after vermutlich keeps the deduction and the negation together.

exercises.english: State that the reader ought to know it cannot be a coincidence.
exercises.german: Der Leser sollte wissen, dass es kein Zufall sein kann.
exercises.why: Sollte in the subordinate clause is the indirect form of a warning about the author's certainty.

exercises.english: Give your personal conclusion that nobody could have known.
exercises.german: Niemand konnte das gewusst haben.
exercises.why: A modal could in the perfect with a universal subject expresses the speaker's belief about knowledge.

exercises.english: Give permission for the guests to wait outside until the room is ready.
exercises.german: Die Gäste dürfen draußen warten, bis der Raum fertig ist.
exercises.why: Dürfen in the second person plural grants permission, with the clause order of a modal verb.

exercises.english: Say politely that you may come in.
exercises.german: Sie dürfen hereinkommen.
exercises.why: A modal of permission addressed to the listener, not a deduction.

exercises.english: Grant permission to park on the pavement for deliveries.
exercises.german: Sie dürfen zum Liefern auf dem Bürgersteig parken.
exercises.why: Dürfen plus an infinitive with a purpose clause states what is allowed.

exercises.english: Ask very politely whether you may ask a short question.
exercises.german: Dürfte ich kurz eine Frage stellen?
exercises.why: Dürfte ich puts the modal in first position and is the standard polite request formula.

exercises.english: Say that taking a photo is probably not allowed in the hall.
exercises.german: Im Foyer dürfte ein Foto wohl nicht erlaubt sein.
exercises.why: Dürfte in the third person softens a rule into an estimate, and wohl adds the hedge.

exercises.english: Grant the visitors permission to use the lift.
exercises.german: Die Besucher dürfen den Aufzug benutzen.
exercises.why: Permission is given to a plural subject with the infinitive at the end.

exercises.english: Say that the addressee may leave early today.
exercises.german: Sie dürfen heute früher gehen.
exercises.why: A separable verb in the final position of a modal clause, as the grammar requires.

exercises.english: Say that you are allowed to take the last seat.
exercises.german: Sie dürfen den letzten Platz nehmen.
exercises.why: Dürfen here follows the pattern of an explicit permission from an authority.

exercises.english: Ask whether one may park here on Sundays.
exercises.german: Darf man sonntags hier parken?
exercises.why: In questions the modal moves to first position and man stands for an unspecified person.

exercises.english: Grant permission to speak briefly after the lecture.
exercises.german: Sie dürfen nach dem Vortrag kurz etwas sagen.
exercises.why: Dürfen plus a temporal clause permits a limited action, not general freedom.

exercises.english: Say that we may probably count on the results by Thursday.
exercises.german: Auf die Ergebnisse können wir wohl bis Donnerstag rechnen.
exercises.why: A modal of possibility combined with rechnen auf reports a justified expectation.

exercises.english: State that the report is probably not finished yet.
exercises.german: Der Bericht dürfte noch nicht fertig sein.
exercises.why: Dürfte plus a negated participle hedges both the state and the negation.

exercises.english: Say that the file can probably still be recovered.
exercises.german: Die Datei müsste sich noch wiederherstellen lassen.
exercises.why: A modal passive states what the speaker believes is still possible, not what he can do.

exercises.english: Grant permission to the interns to sit in on the meeting.
exercises.german: Die Praktikanten dürfen bei der Sitzung zuhören.
exercises.why: Zuhören takes no object, so the accusative case appears only in the separable verb itself.

exercises.english: Say that the tenant may probably keep the flat until March.
exercises.german: Der Mieter dürfte die Wohnung wohl bis März behalten dürfen.
exercises.why: Two instances of dürfen: the outer one hedges, the inner one states the permission.

exercises.english: Ask whether one is allowed to leave the room during the test.
exercises.german: Darf man während der Prüfung den Raum verlassen?
exercises.why: An ob-less yes/no question in the first person singular of the modal permission.

exercises.english: Give permission to the students to use their own notes.
exercises.german: Die Studierenden dürfen ihre eigenen Notizen benutzen.
exercises.why: A permission sentence with a nominalised subject and an accusative object.

exercises.english: Say that we are allowed to park here only on weekdays.
exercises.german: Hier können wir nur werktags parken.
exercises.why: Können here reports what is objectively possible for us, not an epistemic estimate.

exercises.english: Say that the report will presumably have to be rewritten.
exercises.german: Der Bericht wird vermutlich umgeschrieben werden müssen.
exercises.why: A modal passive plus vermutlich: the necessity is attributed to the circumstances, not to a person.

exercises.english: Grant permission to use the lift only in case of fire.
exercises.german: Den Aufzug dürfen Sie nur im Brandfall benutzen.
exercises.why: Permission with a restrictive clause in the infinitive position of a modal sentence.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with apparently: the appointment has obviously been cancelled.
exercises.german: Der Termin ist anscheinend abgesagt.
exercises.why: Anscheinend stands in main-clause position after the subject and marks reported evidence.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with presumably: the invoice has probably not arrived.
exercises.german: Die Rechnung ist vermutlich nicht angekommen.
exercises.why: Vermutlich with a negated participle hedges the whole proposition, not only the verb.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with of course: you obviously have to book earlier.
exercises.german: Natürlich muss man früher buchen.
exercises.why: Natürlich signals that the deduction is obvious, and impersonal man keeps the modal general.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with probably: she is probably not coming to the meeting.
exercises.german: Sie kommt wahrscheinlich nicht zur Besprechung.
exercises.why: Wahrscheinlich before a negated clause hedges the negative without weakening the modal.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with possibly: we might have to change rooms.
exercises.german: Vielleicht müssen wir den Raum wechseln.
exercises.why: Vielleicht marks open possibility, and the modal in first person keeps it non-committal.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with apparently: the server must have crashed.
exercises.german: Der Server ist anscheinend abgestürzt.
exercises.why: Anscheinend with a present perfect reports what the speaker has been told.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with probably: the parcel must be at the post office.
exercises.german: Das Paket muss vermutlich auf der Poststelle sein.
exercises.why: Müssen with a modal adverb after it gives a firm but explicitly estimated conclusion.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with possibly: the workshop might have been moved.
exercises.german: Der Workshop ist vielleicht verlegt worden.
exercises.why: Vielleicht plus a passive perfect covers a change the speaker cannot confirm.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with in all likelihood: the deadline must be extended.
exercises.german: Die Frist muss sehr wahrscheinlich verlängert werden.
exercises.why: Sehr wahrscheinlich intensifies the hedge without changing the modal.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with presumably: the file should still be on the server.
exercises.german: Die Datei sollte vermutlich noch auf dem Server liegen.
exercises.why: Sollte expresses an expectation about the state, vermutlich names it as the speaker's guess.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with maybe: we could come on Friday instead.
exercises.german: Vielleicht könnten wir am Freitag kommen.
exercises.why: Vielleicht with könnte in the first person plural makes the offer easy to refuse.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with of course: nobody can know that for certain.
exercises.german: Natürlich kann das niemand sicher wissen.
exercises.why: The modal is inside a selbst construction, and natürlich marks the conclusion as obvious.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with apparently: the letters have gone to the wrong department.
exercises.german: Die Briefe sind offenbar in die falsche Abteilung gegangen.
exercises.why: Offenbar and anscheinend are interchangeable here; the perfect carries the evidence.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with probably: the train must be running late again.
exercises.german: Der Zug fährt sehr wahrscheinlich wieder mit Verspätung.
exercises.why: A modal adverb plus a present passive hedges a fact the speaker has heard from others.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with possibly: the flat may already be let.
exercises.german: Die Wohnung ist vielleicht schon vermietet.
exercises.why: Vielleicht with a passive states an unverified state, which is exactly what hedging is for.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with apparently: the customer seems to have cancelled.
exercises.german: Der Kunde scheint den Termin abgesagt zu haben.
exercises.why: Scheinen plus a perfect infinitive hedges the whole event through the adverb of seeming.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with it seems: the results must have been manipulated.
exercises.german: Es scheint, dass die Ergebnisse manipuliert worden sein müssen.
exercises.why: A dass-clause after es scheint, dass keeps the modal at the end of the subordinate clause.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with probably: we can probably expect a reply next week.
exercises.german: Wir können wahrscheinlich mit einer Antwort nächste Woche rechnen.
exercises.why: Können mit rechnen auf reports an expectation, and the adverb marks it as likely.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with presumably: you should have received the invoice.
exercises.german: Sie sollten die Rechnung vermutlich erhalten haben.
exercises.why: A perfect with sollten gives an indirect expectation, and vermutlich keeps it a guess.

exercises.skill: Hedging with modal adverbs plus a modal verb
exercises.english: Hedge with maybe: the room must have been booked by someone.
exercises.german: Jemand muss den Raum wohl gebucht haben.
exercises.why: Wohl after the modal softens an otherwise very firm deduction without changing the word order.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: The pupil is very good at maths – state a fact about her skill, not a deduction.
exercises.german: Die Schülerin kann sehr gut rechnen.
exercises.why: Können here is dynamic: it describes an ability the subject actually has.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: The heating is broken and it is minus ten degrees – conclude that it will be cold inside.
exercises.german: Es muss innen kalt werden.
exercises.why: The evidence concerns the heating, so the conclusion about the temperature is epistemic.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: She has swum ten kilometres without stopping – state that she is able to swim that far.
exercises.german: Sie kann zehn Kilometer am Stück schwimmen.
exercises.why: The capacity is demonstrated, so this is a dynamic use of können.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: Nobody knocks and the door does not open – conclude that the door was locked.
exercises.german: Die Tür muss abgeschlossen gewesen sein.
exercises.why: The blocked doorway is the evidence, so the conclusion about the lock is epistemic.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: The doctor is on holiday until Monday – state that she is not available today.
exercises.german: Die Ärztin ist heute nicht zu sprechen.
exercises.why: A fact about the calendar, so no modal is needed at all.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: The notice says the flat is let – conclude that we cannot move in.
exercises.german: Wir können nicht einziehen.
exercises.why: Können here is dynamic: a permission based on the legal situation, not a deduction.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: He holds the national record – conclude that he is the fastest swimmer in the country.
exercises.german: Er muss der schnellste Schwimmer des Landes sein.
exercises.why: From one record the speaker infers a ranking, which is an epistemic conclusion.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: She is allowed to park in that street – state the permission.
exercises.german: Sie darf in dieser Straße parken.
exercises.why: Dürfen is a permission modal addressed to the subject, not a probability.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: The letter has not been opened – conclude that the recipient has not read it.
exercises.german: Der Empfänger muss den Brief nicht gelesen haben.
exercises.why: The conclusion concerns the recipient's action, so the modal is epistemic despite the subject.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: The apprentice has been in the workshop for two years – state that he can work independently.
exercises.german: Der Lehrling kann inzwischen selbstständig arbeiten.
exercises.why: A statement of competence, so können is dynamic and takes no hedging adverb.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: The lights are off and the windows are shuttered – conclude that nobody is home.
exercises.german: Es muss niemand zu Hause sein.
exercises.why: The evidence is the state of the building, so the deduction concerns the residents, not their ability.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: Visitors may take photographs in the atrium – state the permission.
exercises.german: Besucher dürfen im Atrium Fotos machen.
exercises.why: Dürfen states what visitors are allowed to do, an objective permission.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: The test results show a clear trend – conclude that the method works.
exercises.german: Die Methode muss funktionieren.
exercises.why: A deduction from data about how something behaves, so the modal is epistemic.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: She signs all documents with a drawing – state that she cannot write.
exercises.german: Sie kann nicht schreiben.
exercises.why: A lasting incapacity, so können is dynamic and expresses a limitation.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: The parcel weighs twelve kilos and the label says fragile – conclude that it must be treated carefully.
exercises.german: Es muss vorsichtig behandelt werden.
exercises.why: A modal passive expressing an inference about how something must be handled.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: Employees are obliged to wear a badge – state the obligation.
exercises.german: Die Mitarbeiter müssen einen Ausweis tragen.
exercises.why: Müssen expresses a rule that applies to every employee, not the speaker's conclusion.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: The figures do not add up – conclude that there is an error somewhere.
exercises.german: Da muss ein Fehler sein.
exercises.why: The arithmetic is the evidence, so the conclusion about the error is epistemic.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: He has a driving licence – state that he is allowed to drive a car.
exercises.german: Er darf Auto fahren.
exercises.why: A legal permission following from the licence, an objective use of dürfen.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: Nobody in the office has a copy of the contract – conclude that it was never distributed.
exercises.german: Der Vertrag muss nie verteilt worden sein.
exercises.why: The inference concerns a past event, so the modal stays present with a perfect infinitive.

exercises.skill: Epistemic vs dynamic modality, choosing correctly
exercises.english: A beginner cannot read that manual – state the limitation of ability.
exercises.german: Ein Anfänger kann dieses Handbuch nicht lesen.
exercises.why: Können with a negated infinitive expresses a skill limit, a dynamic use.
